doc.title: Chuck Israels interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 11, 2021

title: When a soloist loses the piece
summary: Israels recalls two altos battling at a National Jazz Ensemble concert, Ellington's remark to Jimmy Hamilton, and the Guarneri Quartet.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: Have you ever had a circumstance where a soloist was playing in a fashion that you didn’t feel was contributing to the overall feeling of the piece?
And what do you do about that?

You shut up and live with it usually. It depends on the circumstance. There are circumstances in which you can stop and fix it. Most people don’t do that intentionally but it has happened. It happened at a concert with the National Jazz Ensemble I think in Buffalo, I think it was a concert and Gunther Schuller was there and after the concert I talked to him about it and we both had the same response, and it was a couple of alto saxophone players got into a saxophone battle that might have been — the idea of a kind of back and forth exchange between soloists is not a bad thing — but they lost sight of the — they lost connection with the piece and started playing a bunch of stuff that they’d practiced that sort of fit harmonically but it didn’t. To me I went oh God I wish they’d shut up and stop so we can finish the piece. And I remember someone telling me a real apocryphal or maybe real Ellington quote in which Jimmy Hamilton went to Ellington and said, “Hey it says clarinet solo here but it has no chord changes and stuff.” And Ellington’s response was, “Yeah that’s because I want you to play my piece, not that stuff that you practice.” So, and there’s a balance of that too. Because when I leave open solo space I certainly want a contribution from the personality of the musician who is in that position. They can make enormous contributions that I don’t even think of. They can bring stuff to the music that enlivens it and gives it an immediacy that my written part doesn’t necessarily contain. It contains the opportunity for that because when the Guarneri Quartet sits down and plays a Beethoven quartet they do it in such a way that you believe that they’re making it up. And if they don’t they’re not giving a good performance.
